In the laboratory or clinical settings, indirect calorimetry is 
accomplished using a portable computerized metabolic moni-
tor that can be brought to the bedside or positioned next to a
subject exercising on a treadmill or cycle ergometer. A mask or 
hood is placed over the subject’s face and the amount of air ﬂ ow 
through the lungs per minute (known as minute ventilation) 
is measured by various types of instruments that are built into 
the mask. Gas analyzers in the monitor measure the oxygen 
and carbon dioxide content of both inspired and expired air.
Technological advances have resulted in the development of 
lightweight, portable indirect calorimetry units, which can be
worn by subjects while working or participating in sports. A 
typical unit weighs 2.1 lbs (950 g) and allows accurate testing 
while the subject is engaged in practically any activity at any 
time or location, without being conﬁ ned to an artiﬁ cial labora-
tory environment. In the clinical setting, indirect calorimetry is
recommended as a means to accurately determine the energy 
requirements of critically ill and/or mechanically ventilated 
patients, and to monitor the adequacy and appropriateness of 
nutritional support.
